content.text: You have ten minutes.

Whichever program brought you to Joka, the pace right now is the same for everyone. SIP season is on for the first years, section wars have the whole campus picking sides, and sector prep sessions start in a few days. The pause is not something you find time for once this settles, because it does not settle. You take it, or you do not.
Try This, Breath Awareness

No venue, no mat, no five minutes to spare needed. Sit where you already are. This is box breathing, in for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four. Press begin and follow the circle, not the clock.
Five Minute Sit
No technique this time, just time. Set it, close your eyes, let thoughts pass without following them. Notice how you feel before you pick your phone back up.
Before The Room That Matters

SIP interview, sector prep session, or walking onto the court for section wars, your body is already deciding how the next twenty minutes go before you do. Three small moves change that. Click through them once, then use them for real when it counts.
On Section Wars

Some sections are winning right now, some are not, and both of those things will be forgotten by the time End Terms arrive. What tends to stay is how you showed up, cheered for a teammate, or kept trying after a bad set. Play hard, lose well if you have to, and remember the score is not the point of a team sport, the team is.
This Week's Practice
Three short guided videos, use whichever fits your day.
Myth vs Fact
Meditation means switching your mind off completely.
Meditation is noticing a thought arrived, and not following it. The mind wandering is not failure, it is the rep.
Joka Meditates, IIM Calcutta, twice a week, a little at a time.
One Kilometer to Go
This one's late. Section wars are already old news by now, most of you cooled down days ago, found your regular heart rate again. Fair.
The timing mat catches your feet.It doesn't catch your nervous system.

That keeps running a while after you've stopped: heart still up, breath still short, mind still replaying the last two hundred meters. Same tools work for any workout, any time your body's buzzing louder than your mind can keep up with. Keep this one around.
Loosen the Legs
Four stretches, runner specific. Look up the names if you need a visual, plenty of good demonstrations out there.
Standing, heel to hip. Keeps the front of the thigh from locking up after all that striding.
Hinge at the hips, let the head hang. Releases the back of the leg, where sprint fatigue lands hardest.
Seated, legs straight, spine tall. Resets the lower back after the forward lean of a hard run.
Hip opener, lying down. Undoes the tightness that builds in the hips from repetitive strides.
Bring the Heart Down
Breath is the fastest lever you have over an elevated heart rate. Two ways in.
Breathe in for four counts, out for six. The longer exhale is what tells your nervous system the sprint is over. Six rounds is about a minute.
In for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four. A steady square, useful when the adrenaline is still loud and you need something to count instead of think.
Sit With It

Find the bench. Or the grass. Anywhere you can sit without needing to hold a plank while you do it. Five minutes. Eyes open or closed, your call. First, notice the body exactly as it is. Heart still a little quick. Legs heavy in a good way. Sweat cooling on the back of your neck. Don't change any of it, just notice it's there. Then notice the breath. Not the box, not the count, just the breath as it's already moving, in, out, whatever rhythm it's found on its own. Now let the next thing go. Next match, next class, next deadline, whatever is queued up in your head, let it wait outside for five minutes. It'll still be there. Right now there's just this body, on this bench, breathing.
Keep This One Forever
Everything above is for right after a run. This one is for whenever, an interview waiting room, 2am, five minutes before you walk into a room that matters.

items: Things you can seeReally look, don't just glance. A leaf, a light, a crack in the pavement.
Things you can feelThe bench under you, fabric against skin, the ground under your feet.
Things you can hearTraffic, wind, your own breathing.

content.text: By the time you've found all ten, your mind has stopped spinning and come back into the room. This one works anywhere. Keep it.

None of this expires when the section war ends. Bring it to your next run, your next workout, your next hard morning. And if you'd rather sit with people than sit alone, we're around twice a week, come find us.

title: The Month of Restraint
subtitle: Saavan asks you to do less. That turns out to be the hard part.

content.text: The Month of Restraint
Shravan arrives with the rain and a strange instruction: eat lighter, sit longer, want less. In a term where everything is asking for more of you, that lands oddly.
The month isn't asking you to add a practice.It's asking you to subtract noise.
Below: why the season works this way, what to eat and skip, two asanas, a breathing visualization, playlists to sit with, and an argument for being bored on purpose.
Why Saavan Works This Way

The monsoon logic is older than any of us and fairly practical underneath the ritual. Humidity climbs, sunlight drops, and digestion genuinely slows. Traditional practice reads that as a signal: this is not the season for heavy food, hard travel, or scattered energy. So the month turns inward instead. Lighter meals. More chanting. More sitting. Less of everything that pulls outward. Shravan is the one month in the calendar that treats restraint as the practice itself, rather than as preparation for something else. You do not need to hold any particular belief for the structure to be useful. A month of deliberately doing less, right as the term gets heaviest, is a good idea on its own terms.
Fasting, Honestly
Saavan fasting is observance before it is anything else. Mondays are the traditional day, and the forms people keep vary widely.
Some keep a full fast on Mondays. Some eat one simple meal. Some only drop grains, or salt, or anything non-vegetarian for the month. All of these count. There is no leaderboard here.
The point is not the empty stomach. It is noticing how loudly the body asks, how quickly the mind negotiates, and choosing anyway. That noticing is the practice. The food is just the setting.
If a food fast isn't for you, keep the shape and change the object. A day without screens after 9pm. A day without complaining. Same muscle, different weight.

Please skip food fasting entirely if you have any medical reason to, are on medication that needs food, or have any history of disordered eating. Talk to a doctor rather than to us. The screen version above works just as well.
Eating With the Weather
Principles, not a plan. Monsoon digestion is slower and the campus water table is doing what it does every year.

items: 01 Warm over cold, cooked over rawSalads and cold food sit heavier this season than they look. Cooked and warm moves easier.
02 Careful with leafy greensTraditionally avoided through Shravan, and the reasoning holds up: they hold moisture and contamination through a wet month.
03 Ginger, turmeric, black pepper, ajwainThe standard monsoon kitchen. They earn their place by helping a slow gut along.
04 Water that has been boiledThe least spiritual line in this issue and possibly the most useful one.
05 Stop a little before fullThe oldest instruction in the book, and the one nobody follows. Try it for a week.

content.text: Be Bored On Purpose

Here is the part that will feel wrong. Every gap in your day is currently filled. The walk to class, the queue at the mess, the ninety seconds before a lecture starts, all of it goes to a screen. Nothing in that is unusual and nobody is being scolded here. But it means the mind has not been genuinely unoccupied in a long time, possibly years. Idle and distracted are not the same thing. Scrolling is not rest, it is a different kind of work. Actual idleness, sitting with nothing happening and not reaching for anything, is where attention slowly repairs itself. It feels unbearable for the first few minutes and then it does not. The practical case is straightforward. The ability to hold attention on one thing for a long stretch is getting rarer every year. Whatever you end up doing after this campus, that will be worth more than it is today, precisely because fewer people will have it. So this month, leave one gap empty. Do not fill the queue. Do not fill the walk. Let it be boring on purpose and see what your head does with the room.
Three minutes. Phone face down, nothing playing, nothing to look at. That is the whole exercise.
Two Asanas for a Wet Month
Both are seated, both help a sluggish monsoon digestion, and both can be done in a hostel room without moving furniture.

Kneel, sit back on the heels, spine tall, hands on thighs. The one pose traditionally done straight after eating rather than before. Five to ten minutes post-meal is the classic prescription for exactly the heaviness this season brings.

Lie on your back, draw one knee across the body, let the head turn the other way, hold and breathe. A gentle wring for the middle of the body. Do both sides, a minute or two each, and it works well right before sleep.
The Rain Breath
A breathing visualization built for the season. Four counts in, two to hold, six out, with something to picture on each phase.

phases.label: Breathe in
phases.cue: Rain gathering. Draw it up from the ground, all the way to the top of the chest.

phases.label: Hold
phases.cue: The pause before it falls. Everything held, nothing moving.

phases.label: Breathe out
phases.cue: Let it fall. Slow, long, all the way down and out through the floor.

One for chanting along, one for sitting quietly, one for guided practice. All three will keep growing through the month.

What We're Reading

The CEO Mindset, currently doing the rounds among a few of us. The thread worth pulling on for this issue: the discipline that compounds is rarely the dramatic kind. It is the small refusal, repeated, on the days it does not feel like it matters. Which is more or less what Shravan has been saying for a few thousand years, in different words. If you are reading something that fits the month, tell us and it goes in the next issue.

Pick one thing from this issue. Not five. One Monday, one asana, one empty gap in the day left unfilled. Restraint does not scale by doing more of it at once, which is rather the point. And if you would rather sit with people than sit alone, we are around twice a week. Come find us.

title: The Third Quotient
subtitle: This campus trains you hard for one kind of intelligence. Nobody grades the other two.

content.text: The Third Quotient
Every case, every cold call, every mid-term here is built to sharpen one thing. It matters. It just isn't the only thing that matters.
The other two intelligences don't show up on a transcript. They show up in the interview, the rejection, the 2am spiral before a submission. This issue is about training for those too.
The Three Quotients
Logic, pattern, recall. The kind of intelligence a classroom is built to measure.

Reading and regulating emotion, yours and the room's. It's the difference between a case interview that goes well and one that doesn't, and it's usually the real cause when a team falls apart, not the deadline. One way to build it: name what you're feeling before you react to it. That half-second gap is most of the skill.

The least familiar of the three. Not religion. The capacity to sit with uncertainty without needing to resolve it immediately, and to know what you're actually optimizing for beyond the next number on a stipend letter. Hardest to explain, most useful under pressure.
Your Feed Is Training Data

You audit your diet this month already. Audit what you follow too. What shows up in your feed daily becomes the default shape of your thoughts, whether you notice it happening or not. Unfollow whatever leaves you comparing or resentful, even if it's entertaining in the moment. Follow what leaves you calmer or sharper. Put good out where you can, it tends to find its way back, not as karma bookkeeping, just as how people and rooms actually work.
Move, Even for Ten Minutes

Start small. Ten minutes, a short walk, a stretch, anything. Don't wait for the ideal routine before beginning, the bar for day one should be embarrassingly low. You'll regret every week you didn't start, once you're a few weeks into actually doing it. That's the whole pitch. Start, then build from there.
Nadi Shodhana
Alternate nostril breathing, the classical technique for balancing exactly the split this issue is about, one side active, one side still.
Right thumb closes the right nostril, breathe in left. Close left with the ring finger, release right, breathe out right. In right, close right, breathe out left. That's one round.
The Playlists
The same three from last issue, still growing, and the guided breathwork one pairs directly with the practice above.

title: Nobody's Got This Figured Out
subtitle: The people who look calmest right now are usually just better at hiding it.

content.text: Nobody's Got This Figured Out
This term is genuinely heavier than most, coursework stacking on top of SIP deliverables still being wrapped up, and it's landing at the same time for almost everyone in your batch.
You're allowed to struggle. So is everyone around you.
Nobody's grade reflects how many nights they lay awake before it. Worth remembering the next time a rank list makes you feel like you're the only one struggling.
People
You're Not Supposed to Do This Alone

The instinct under pressure is to disappear into the syllabus and cut everything else out. That's the wrong move. A five-minute call home, a message to a senior who's already been through this exact term, ten minutes with a friend who isn't even talking about exams, none of it costs you study time in any way that matters. You don't have to carry this by yourself.

Seniors especially. Someone in the batch above has sat exactly where you're sitting, with the exact same panic, less than a year ago. Ask them something small if asking something big feels like too much.
Outlet
Keep One Thing That Isn't Studying

Whatever it is, sport, music, a show, cooking, don't let this term take it away entirely. The people who white-knuckle through exam season with zero outlet burn out faster and recover slower than the people who protect even twenty minutes a day for something that has nothing to do with grades. You are not just a rank on a list. Keep proving that to yourself, especially this term.
Body
Move Every Day, a Little More Than Yesterday

content.title: Walking counts
content.body: A short walk between study blocks does more for a stuck brain than another twenty minutes at the desk usually will.

content.title: Cardio, in short bursts
content.body: Doesn't need to be long. Ten minutes of getting the heart rate up is enough to count for the day.

content.title: Bodyweight, zero equipment
content.body: Squats, push-ups, a plank, right there in your room. Increase it slightly every day rather than staying flat.

content.text: Blood moving through the body clears the head in a way a longer study session can't. And there's a real, felt confidence in watching yourself do a little more this week than last week, one that carries into the exam room better than the syllabus alone ever does.
Fuel
Eat Like It Matters, Most of the Time

Health is the actual priority here, not a side quest to studying. Regular meals, real food more often than not, water instead of another coffee when you're not sure which one you actually need.

An occasional indulgence, the 2am maggi, the celebratory dessert, is completely fine and not something to feel bad about. The pattern is what matters, not any single meal.
Perspective
Three Teachers on the Same Problem
Different traditions, same underlying question: how do you stop suffering from wanting things to be other than they are.

content.name: Gautam Buddha
content.body: Built his entire teaching around one observation: suffering comes from clinging, to outcomes, to comparisons, to a version of events that hasn't happened yet. The exam result you're anxious about right now is a future you're gripping before it exists. Loosening that grip doesn't mean not caring, it means not adding a second layer of suffering on top of the studying you're already doing.

content.name: Mahavira
content.body: Taught a discipline of the self so total that his own life is the proof of concept, extreme self-command, built one small act of restraint at a time. The relevant piece for this term isn't the extremity, it's the method: discipline is built in small repeated choices, not in one heroic push the night before an exam.

content.name: Osho
content.body: Spent much of his teaching arguing against exactly what most people assume meditation is, sitting still, forcing the mind blank, waiting for peace to arrive. He pushed the opposite: that stillness on the other side of real intensity, movement, breath, even sound, often works better for a modern, wired-up mind than sitting silently ever could. Which sets up the next section.

content.text: Practice
Meditation Isn't Doing Nothing

The image most people have, sitting cross-legged, mind empty, is one specific technique, not the definition of the whole thing. Meditation is closer to full, undistracted awareness, and awareness doesn't always need stillness to arrive. Sometimes the body has to work something out first.

phases.label: Shake it out
phases.cue: Loose, fast, whole body. No shape to it, just get it moving.

phases.label: Bigger movement
phases.cue: Arms, legs, in place. Let the heart rate climb.

phases.label: Let it out
phases.cue: One loud exhale. A sound if you want one. Then stop.

phases.label: Freeze
phases.cue: Completely still. Notice the heart still going.

phases.label: Let it settle
phases.cue: Eyes closed or soft gaze. Just watch what is left.

content.text: Pick one thing from this issue, not all six. The exam doesn't care which one you pick. Your term will go better either way.

title: Staying Calm Through Placements
subtitle: A few things that help you stay steady through the process. Take whatever is useful.

content.text: Staying Calm Through Placements

You have already come through SIP preparation and a run of buddy calls. Some might not have received shortlists yet, but they will receive them in the coming days. Here are a few things that help you stay steady through the process. Take whatever is useful.
Written for the juniors going into final placements. Other batches can use it too.
Food
Eat Light, Eat Sattvic

On interview days, keep food light all day. Fruits, coconut water and an electrolyte drink are enough for most people. Skip anything oily, heavy or spicy, and go easy on tamasic and rajasic food, which includes the third cup of coffee. Sattvic food keeps the mind calm, and a calm mind answers better.
Breath
Breathe

Here are two guided breathwork sessions, 20 minutes each, to start with. They are only two of the many that exist, so search YouTube for one that fits what you need, whether that is calming down, sleeping better or settling your nerves before a big day. Do one in your room before the process starts, with headphones on and your phone on silent.

content.text: Habits
Small Habits That Help

content.title: Move a little every day
content.body: Stretching or a short workout in your room is enough.

content.title: Sleep properly the night before
content.body: Tired people speak faster and think worse.

content.title: Reset between rounds
content.body: Two minutes of slow breaths, feet on the floor, phone away.

content.title: Talk to someone
content.body: Friends, seniors, professors. Asking early is easier than asking late.

content.title: Use AI as a practice partner
content.body: Mock interviews, case drills, random GD topics and feedback on your answers. Practise with it, but do not memorise scripts.

content.title: Mute the batch groups
content.body: For a few hours a day.

content.text: Results
When the Results Come

You will see friends get placed while you are still waiting, and you may get rejected yourself. If you take it personally, it only gets worse. Keep calm and do your best. You have a lot left to do in life, and this process does not decide it. Rejection is part of every career, including the ones that look smooth from the outside.
If you get placed, help your friends who have not been placed yet. Share what worked, run a mock with them, and sit with them after a bad round.
And bring the section war spirit. Back your section in every round, and back every IIMC student, whatever their section.
All the best, and take care.
